headlines.article_text: Qualcomm sinks after earnings, leading postelection chip sell-off Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Companies tied to the AI buildout are all selling off as concerns mount about a slowdown following the midterm elections. The Nasdaq headed for its worst day since April 2025. Chipmakers like AMD, Micron and Applied Materials all suffered double-digit percentage drops. In this article QCOM AMD NVDA INTC ARM MU Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 3:12 03:12 Qualcomm's data center business barely offsetting losses in smartphones: Seaport's Jay Goldberg Closing Bell: Overtime Chipmakers plummeted on Thursday, with Nvidia pushing the Nasdaq toward its worst day in 19 months, after this week's midterm election results raised concerns on Wall Street that the artificial intelligence buildout is poised to slow down. Neoclouds like CoreWeave tumbled for a second straight day. Qualcomm contributed to the selloff after issuing a disappointing earnings forecast for the current quarter. Qualcomm and Nvidia both dropped about 8%. The environment has gone from bad to worse for companies intimately tied to AI infrastructure, as the combination of rising interest rates, ballooning capital needs and the Democratic sweep in Congress has led to increased fears that wide swaths of the market are going to be weighed down by too much debt and too little revenue. Advanced Micro Devices , Micron and Applied Materials all suffered double-digit percentage losses on Thursday. Elon Musk , who contributed hundreds of millions of dollars to try and get Republicans elected in Texas and elsewhere, saw shares of his public companies, SpaceX and Tesla , tumble 7% and 10%, respectively. In Tuesday's election, the states with the most ambitious AI data center plans all turned blue. Democrats won key contests for governor and the Senate in Texas and Ohio, while also coming up victorious in the gubernatorial race in Georgia, where Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff also cruised to reelection. There were 41 local ballot measures in 10 states up for a vote on Tuesday that would place restrictions on the construction of data centers in different ways, according to Ballotpedia . Voters sided against data centers in each measure except one in Harwood, North Dakota, according to an analysis by Ballotpedia and additional results gathered by CNBC on Wednesday. On Wednesday night, at the Wall Street Journal Tech conference, Meta President Dina Powell McCormick told the audience that building data centers is "going to be harder" following the elections. She added that one of the victorious governors had said that, "As soon as we get past the inauguration, let's meet because we don't want to lose this investment in our town. We don't want these jobs to go elsewhere," according to the Journal. Meta, like its hyperscaler peers — Alphabet , Amazon and Microsoft — has laid out an ambitious path for infrastructure development, with spending plans that extend well past $100 billion a year. Meta went free cash flow negative in the latest quarter, joining Alphabet and Amazon, which turned negative in the prior period. Qualcomm stock chart. Qualcomm on Wednesday became the latest chipmaker to report booming growth in its data center business, though it's still a relatively small unit for the company. Qualcomm had $650 million in data center revenue during the quarter, mostly from customizing and connectivity work, CEO Cristiano Amon said. "We don't have a demand issue; it's a supply issue," Amon told CNBC in an interview. "If I had more supply, I would probably be doing better." The problem for Qualcomm and fellow chipmakers Intel and AMD is that the global memory shortage is jacking up prices, making it harder to get key supplies and leading to surging prices for consumer devices. Intel last week reported a 78% jump in data center revenue, but the stock got crushed due to a weaker-than-expected forecast from the memory shortage. And AMD said this week that sales in its data center business more than doubled in the latest period. Investors are looking past the numbers and questioning the sustainability of that growth, and whether buyers of the technology will be able to put it all to use. "There's going to be a knee-jerk reaction, and that could lead to some delays, and that's going to be some concerns, " Richard Clode, a portfolio manager at Janus Henderson, told "Squawk on the Street." "We're not going to solve for that in terms of knowing the answers to that anytime soon, unfortunately." — CNBC's MacKenzie Sigalos contributed to this report. Joe Skipper | Reuters Jeff Bezos ' Blue Origin has delayed a return to flight for its flagship New Glenn rocket to January 2027, later than its earlier target of the end of this year, as it rushes to recover from a major explosion in May. Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp told employees in a memo Wednesday that the company's launch timing slipped as a result of delays with reconstructing its Cape Canaveral launch pad, including bad weather over the summer. "This small adjustment doesn't diminish what we've accomplished or the importance of the work still ahead," Limp wrote in the memo, which was viewed by CNBC. "Returning New Glenn to flight remains our top priority — it's worth it." The Financial Times earlier reported the memo. The January 2027 timeframe is about 10 days later than Blue Origin's earlier launch target, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC, who spoke on condition of anonymity in order to discuss internal matters. The New Glenn explosion in May, which occurred during a hot-fire test, badly damaged Blue Origin's Florida launchpad. The company was slated to deploy 48 satellites for Amazon 's Leo internet-from-space service just a few days later. Since then, the company has moved swiftly to repair the launch facility and reworked its pad configuration. Bezos told Fox News last month that the company was still expecting New Glenn to fly again in December. The mishap was inconveniently timed, as Blue Origin has been working to ramp up its launch cadence in an effort to compete with its chief rival, Elon Musk 's SpaceX , for commercial and government customers. The New Glenn delays have hampered Amazon's Leo constellation buildout, for which it relies on Blue Origin for a portion of its launches. Amazon has turned to other providers, including United Launch Alliance and Arianespace, in the interim, especially as SpaceX has phased out Falcon 9 launches to prioritize testing its enormous Starship rocket.
